subsection: 3. Case study: the elections of 1885 and 1886 — issues and outcomes

notes.h: Background: the franchise and the seats (1884–1885)
notes.b: Two Acts changed the electorate and the constituencies just before the 1885 election, and the Irish Party was the main beneficiary.
points: The Representation of the People Act 1884, the Third Reform Act, extended the household franchise of the boroughs to county voters, including agricultural labourers in Britain and Ireland.
In Ireland the Third Reform Act more than tripled the electorate, from roughly 230,000 voters to about 740,000 (about, as figures vary by source).
The Redistribution of Seats Act 1885 divided most Irish seats into single-member constituencies, which made it easier for a national party to win by majorities in rural areas.
The new Irish rural electorate was largely tenant farmers and labourers, many organised through the National League and the Catholic clergy.
The Irish party’s organisation, built through the National League and Parnell’s pledge system, was ready to select candidates in almost every constituency by the autumn of 1885.
Joseph Chamberlain’s Central Board scheme of 1884, which proposed elected bodies to run Irish local government, was offered as an alternative to Home Rule and rejected by Parnell.

notes.b: Parnell’s party selected candidates through local conventions, and Parnell used the balance of power to press for Home Rule and land reform.
points: Candidates were chosen at National League conventions, where the local clergy often had a strong voice in deciding who would stand.
Parnell’s party aimed to win a bloc of seats that would hold the balance between the Liberals and the Conservatives at Westminster.
In June 1885 the Irish party voted with the Conservatives to defeat Gladstone’s Liberal government on its budget, and Lord Salisbury took office as a minority Conservative prime minister.
Historians debate how far Parnell reached a formal understanding with Salisbury’s Conservatives in 1885, which the Ashbourne Act of 1885 may have reflected.
In the general election campaign Parnell told Irish voters in English and Scottish seats to vote against the Liberal candidates, which helped the Conservatives in several British constituencies.

notes.b: The election returned a Parliament with no clear majority, and the Irish Party won almost every Catholic seat outside east Ulster.
points: The general election was held in November and December 1885, and the Irish Party won about 86 of the 103 Irish seats.
The Irish Party won nearly every seat in Catholic-majority areas, from Munster and Connacht to most of Leinster and Ulster outside its eastern counties.
In east Ulster, unionist candidates won most seats, including the Belfast constituencies, which showed the division between nationalist and unionist Ireland.
The results across the United Kingdom were approximately Liberal 335, Conservative 249 and Irish Party 86, so no party had a majority of the 670 seats.
The hung Parliament gave the Irish Party the decisive vote, and both main parties needed its support to govern.
Gladstone had not yet declared himself in favour of Home Rule when the election was held, but he was already moving towards the policy.
Dublin University, the Trinity College seat, continued to return unionist MPs, so the Irish Party did not win every Irish constituency.
Parnell was returned for Cork City at the 1885 election, and he sat for that seat until his death in 1891.

notes.h: The Hawarden Kite and Gladstone’s conversion (December 1885)
notes.b: In December 1885 the Liberal leader’s conversion to Home Rule was leaked, and it reshaped British politics.
points: The Hawarden Kite was a press report in December 1885 that Gladstone, at his home Hawarden in Wales, had become convinced of the need for Home Rule for Ireland.
The report appeared in the press before Gladstone had made any public declaration, which allowed him to test opinion without committing himself formally.
Gladstone’s conversion shocked many Liberals, and Lord Hartington, the Whig leader, and Joseph Chamberlain opposed it.
Gladstone’s conversion gave Parnell’s party a route to Home Rule through the Liberal party, which the Conservatives could not offer.

notes.h: The fall of Salisbury and the First Home Rule Bill (January–April 1886)
notes.b: Salisbury’s government fell in January 1886, and Gladstone introduced a Home Rule bill in April that split his own party.
points: Salisbury’s minority government was defeated in the Commons in January 1886, after the Irish Party voted against it, and Gladstone formed his third ministry in February.
Lord Randolph Churchill, a Conservative, opposed Home Rule and in February 1886 told a Belfast audience that Ulster would fight and Ulster would be right.
Gladstone introduced the First Home Rule Bill on 8 April 1886, which would have created an Irish legislature in Dublin with an executive responsible to it.
Under the bill Irish MPs would no longer sit at Westminster, and Ireland would contribute to the costs of imperial services.
Gladstone introduced an Irish Land Purchase Bill in the same session, to provide state loans for tenants to buy their farms.
Joseph Chamberlain resigned from the cabinet in March 1886 over Home Rule, and the Liberal party divided over the bill.

notes.h: Defeat of the bill and the 1886 election
notes.b: The Commons rejected the bill in June 1886, and the July election gave a majority to the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists.
points: The Liberal Unionists, led by Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington, opposed the bill, and about 90 Liberal MPs voted against it in the June division.
The Home Rule Bill was defeated at second reading on 8 June 1886 by 343 votes to 313, a majority of 30.
Gladstone dissolved Parliament and called a general election, which was held in July 1886.
The election produced a majority for the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists combined, and Lord Salisbury formed his second government.
The 1886 election reinforced the Irish Party’s position in Ireland, where it again won most nationalist seats, and Home Rule was postponed until 1893.

notes.h: Unionist mobilisation: the Orange card and Belfast (1886)
notes.b: Unionists in Ulster organised against Home Rule, and the Belfast riots of 1886 showed the sectarian edge of the crisis.
points: Lord Randolph Churchill’s use of the Orange card, the appeal to Ulster Protestants, helped to mobilise unionist opinion in the province.
Unionist leaders in Belfast and the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union, founded in 1885, mobilised opposition through meetings, petitions and newspapers such as the Belfast News-Letter.
The Belfast riots of July–August 1886 followed the expulsion of Catholic workers from the shipyards and engineering works, and about thirty people were killed (about).
The Belfast violence led to a sharp division between Protestant and Catholic communities in the city, and it was used by both sides as evidence for their case.

notes.h: Key personality: Charles Stewart Parnell (role in the 1885–1886 elections)
notes.b: In this case study Parnell was the central figure: he made the Irish Party a decisive force and he tied Home Rule to the Liberal party.
points: As the leader of the Irish Party, Parnell chose the strategy of holding the balance of power in the 1885 Parliament rather than aligning with either major party.
Parnell was a participant who organised the candidate selection, but he did not control every local decision, since the clergy and local branches also shaped it.
Contemporary nationalists saw the 1885 result as the triumph of Parnell’s leadership, and the Irish Party’s majority of seats as a national mandate.
Contemporary unionists and some Liberals saw Parnell as a dangerous leader who had made Home Rule a price for the Liberals’ support.
Historians differ over Parnell’s dealings with the Conservatives in 1885; they agree that his strategy brought Home Rule closer to the centre of British politics.

notes.h: Documents and the views of each side
notes.b: Contemporary speeches, newspapers and cartoons reflected the different positions of nationalists, unionists, Liberals and Conservatives.
points: Nationalist newspapers, such as the Freeman’s Journal, presented the election as a national victory and Home Rule as a settled demand of the Irish people.
Unionist newspapers, such as the Belfast News-Letter, described Home Rule as a threat to the empire and to Protestant interests in Ulster.

Punch was largely hostile to Gladstone’s Home Rule policy, and its cartoons presented Parnell as a threat to the empire, while pro-Home Rule cartoons appeared mainly in nationalist and some London newspapers.
A document from 1885 or 1886 is best placed by its stage: the election campaign, the Hawarden Kite, the debates on the April bill, or the June division and July election.
Speeches by Gladstone argued that Home Rule would restore peace and bring Irish loyalty to the empire, while critics argued that it would lead to the break-up of the United Kingdom.
Liberal Unionist speeches, notably by Chamberlain, argued that an Irish parliament would threaten the rights of the Ulster minority and the imperial connection.

notes.b: The 1885–1886 elections fixed Home Rule as the central Irish question in British politics and created organised unionism.
points: Home Rule was tied to the Liberal party from 1886, and the Liberals kept it as a central policy until the Third Home Rule Act was placed on the statute book in 1914.
The Irish Party’s majority in 1885 was the high point of Parnell’s leadership, but it was followed by the O’Shea scandal of 1890 and the split in the party.
The Liberal Unionists, who joined the Conservatives in 1886, became a permanent party of opposition to Home Rule and of the Union.
Organised unionism, through the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union and the Ulster organisations, took shape in these years and developed into the Ulster Unionist movement.
The 1886 defeat showed that a Home Rule bill could not pass without Liberal and Irish unity, which set the pattern for the Second and Third Home Rule Bills.
Historians see 1885–86 as a turning point, when the British parties began to divide over Ireland along lines that lasted until the 1920s.

notes.b: Judgements on the case study compare the Irish Party’s achievements with the limits of a single bill and a single election.
points: Achievement: the Irish Party won a national mandate, and its votes and the pressure of the election helped to bring Gladstone to adopt Home Rule as government policy.
Limit: the First Home Rule Bill failed in the Commons, and Parnell’s party had no means to pass legislation without a Liberal majority.
Contemporary nationalists judged the defeat a betrayal by the Liberal Unionists, while later historians tend to see it as a result of unionist opposition and the Liberal split.
The Liberal split was a success for the unionists, but it also showed the limits of the unionist case in Catholic Ireland.

keyTerms.definition: The demand for an Irish parliament in Dublin to manage Irish domestic affairs, which was the central question of the 1885–86 elections.
Government through elected representatives, which the Third Reform Act of 1884 widened by giving the vote to county householders.
The Representation of the People Act 1884, which extended the household franchise to county voters and greatly enlarged the Irish electorate.
The Act that redrew most constituencies as single-member seats, which made the 1885 election the first on the new boundaries.
A position in which a small party holds the decisive votes in a hung Parliament, allowing it to choose which main party governs.
A Parliament in which no single party has an overall majority, so a smaller party such as the Irish Party can decide the outcome.
The December 1885 press report that Gladstone had become convinced of Home Rule, leaked before he made a public declaration.
The Liberals led by Joseph Chamberlain and Lord Hartington who opposed the First Home Rule Bill and joined the Conservatives in 1886.
The appeal to Protestant and unionist loyalty in Ulster, used by Lord Randolph Churchill to mobilise opposition to Home Rule.
